questions.q: Six children of heights 138, 145, 131, 140, 127, 136 cm stand in this order. Each says how many of the children standing next to her or him are taller. What do they say, from the left?
Six children of six different heights stand in a line and call out how many taller neighbours they have. Which of these calls, read from the left, can really happen?
Meena stands at the right end of a line of children. She says she called '2' because both children next to her are taller. What is wrong with her claim?
questions.a: She has just one neighbour, so she can call at most 1
o: She has just one neighbour, so she can call at most 1
She must be the tallest child, and the tallest child always calls 2
Equal-height neighbours do count as taller, so she should call 1
Only a child in the middle of the line can ever call 0 in a line

questions.q: Five children stand in a line with heights 140, 140, 150, 140, 140 cm. Using the rule 'count only neighbours who are taller', what do they call, from the left?
A teacher adds up all the calls made by the 9 children of different heights in a line. She finds the total does not change however she rearranges them. What is the total?

Five children of five different heights stand in a line and call their taller-neighbour counts.
Statement 1: The calls 0, 1, 1, 1, 1 can be made.
Statement 2: The calls 1, 2, 1, 2, 0 can be made.
Statement 3: Two children standing next to each other can never both call 2.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In a line of children of different heights, the shortest child always calls 2.
Reason (R): Every child standing next to the shortest child is taller than her.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: At most ___ children, in a line of 8 children of different heights, can call '2'.

Five children of heights 120, 135, 128, 142, 125 cm stand in this order. (a) Write the calls from the left. (b) The first two children now swap places. Which children's calls change, and what is the new list of calls?
questions.a: (a) 1, 0, 2, 0, 1. (b) The new order is 135, 120, 128, 142, 125; the calls are 0, 2, 1, 0, 1. The calls of the first three children change; the last two stay 0 and 1.
s: Part (b): new calls 0, 2, 1, 0, 1 with the first three children changed

questions.q: (a) Why can a child standing at an end of the line call only 0 or 1? (b) Using this, find the largest number of children who can call '2' in a line of 3 children of different heights.
questions.a: (a) An end child has only one neighbour, so the count of taller neighbours cannot exceed 1. (b) Only the middle child can call 2, so the largest number is 1 (she must be the shortest of the three).
s: Part (a): an end child has one neighbour, so at most 1
Part (b): only the middle child can call 2, so the answer is 1

questions.q: True or False: If every child in a line calls 0, the children in that line must all be of the same height.
questions.a: True. If two neighbours differed in height, the shorter of them would have a taller neighbour and would call at least 1. So every pair of neighbours must be equal, and the whole line is of one height.
s: Reason: a shorter child beside a taller one cannot call 0, so no neighbours can differ

questions.q: True or False: Five children of different heights can call four 1s and one 0 only if they stand in order of increasing height.
questions.a: False. The calls 1, 1, 0, 1, 1 are also possible: heights 1, 2, 5, 4, 3 (any units) rise to the tallest in the middle and fall after it, and each child other than the tallest has exactly one taller neighbour. Decreasing order also works.
s: Corrects it: the tallest can stand in the middle (or at the left end) with heights rising to her and then falling

questions.q: Tanvi says: 'In our group of 6 children of different heights, I called 2 and the friend standing next to me also called 2.' Decide whether this can happen and say why.
questions.a: It cannot happen. A child who calls 2 is shorter than both neighbours; if the friend beside her also calls 2, each of them would be shorter than the other, which is impossible for children of different heights.
s: Reason: each would have to be shorter than the other

questions.q: Ritu claims that in a line of 7 children of different heights, 3 children can call '2'. Test her claim by giving an arrangement of heights 126, 128, 131, 135, 142, 145 and 150 cm.
questions.a: Ritu is right. Put the three shortest (126, 128, 131) at the 2nd, 4th and 6th places and the four taller at the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th, for example 135, 126, 142, 128, 145, 131, 150. Calls: 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, so three children call 2.
s: Gives a valid arrangement with the shortest three in the 2nd, 4th and 6th places
States that her claim is correct

questions.q: Show that no line of 4 children of different heights can make the calls 0, 2, 2, 0.
questions.a: The 2nd and 3rd children both call 2, so the 2nd is shorter than the 3rd and the 3rd is shorter than the 2nd. Both cannot hold. So the calls 0, 2, 2, 0 cannot happen.
s: Notes that the 2nd and 3rd children are neighbours who both call 2
Shows the 2nd must be shorter than the 3rd and the 3rd shorter than the 2nd

questions.q: Six children of heights 126, 128, 131, 135, 142 and 150 cm stand first from the shortest to the tallest, and then from the tallest to the shortest. Write the calls in both lines and say what the two lists have in common.
questions.a: Increasing: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0. Decreasing: 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. Both lists have five 1s and one 0; the 0 belongs to the tallest child, and the lists are mirror images.
s: Common: five 1s, one 0, the 0 is the tallest child

questions.q: Seven children of heights 131, 142, 128, 150, 135, 126, 145 cm stand in this order and call their taller-neighbour counts. (a) Write the calls. (b) Which child is the tallest, and what does she call? (c) Rearrange the same seven children so that as many as possible call 2, and write the calls. (d) Explain why no arrangement can give more than that many 2s.
questions.a: (a) 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0. (b) 150 cm calls 0, as the tallest has no taller neighbour. (c) For example 135, 126, 142, 128, 145, 131, 150 gives 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, three 2s. (d) A '2' needs two neighbours, so the end places are out, and two 2s cannot be next to each other; among places 2 to 6 at most 3 non-adjacent places can be chosen.
s: Part (a): the seven calls written correctly
Part (d): ends cannot call 2 and neighbours cannot both call 2, so at most 3

questions.q: Five children of different heights (call them 1 to 5, with 5 the tallest) stand in a line. A child calls 0 when no neighbour is taller. (a) Arrange them so that exactly one child calls 0. (b) Arrange them so that exactly three call 0. (c) Explain why the number of children calling 0 can never be 4 or 5. (d) Explain why it can never be 0.
questions.a: (a) Increasing order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 gives 1, 1, 1, 1, 0: only the tallest calls 0. (b) 4, 1, 5, 2, 3 gives 0, 2, 0, 2, 0: three call 0. (c) Two neighbouring children cannot both call 0, since the shorter of the two would have a taller neighbour; so 0-callers are not next to each other and at most 3 of 5 places can be used. (d) The tallest child has no taller neighbour, so at least one child always calls 0.
s: Part (a): an arrangement with exactly one 0, shown by its calls
Part (b): an arrangement with exactly three 0s, shown by its calls
Part (c): neighbours cannot both call 0, so at most 3 in 5 places
Part (d): the tallest child always calls 0

questions.q: At a school assembly, six children of heights 134, 141, 129, 138, 125, 143 cm stand in this order and each calls the number of taller neighbours. (a) Write the six calls. (b) Which children call 2? (c) The PT teacher then lines them from the shortest to the tallest. Write the new calls. (d) In a game each child scores the number she called, and the teacher also wants as few children as possible to score 0. Compare the total scores of the two lines and recommend a line.
questions.a: (a) 1, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0. (b) The children of 129 cm and 125 cm. (c) 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0. (d) Both lines total 5 points, so the scores tie. The given line has three children scoring 0 and the increasing line has one, so she should use the increasing line.
s: Part (b): the 129 cm and 125 cm children
Part (d): both totals 5, zeros 3 against 1, recommends the increasing line

questions.q: A nursery has five saplings of heights 41, 52, 36, 58 and 47 cm planted in a row in this order. Taller neighbours shade a sapling and save water. Use these rules: a sapling that has 2 taller neighbours saves 3 litres a day, one with 1 taller neighbour saves 1 litre a day, one with none saves nothing. Water costs ₹1.5 a litre. Replanting costs ₹120. (a) Write the number of taller neighbours for each sapling in the present row. (b) Find the water saved a day in the present row. (c) Replant them as 58, 36, 52, 41, 47 and find the water saved a day. (d) The dry season lasts 60 days. Is replanting worth it? Give the break-even number of days.
questions.a: (a) 1, 0, 2, 0, 1. (b) 1 + 0 + 3 + 0 + 1 = 5 litres. (c) calls 0, 2, 0, 2, 0: 0 + 3 + 0 + 3 + 0 = 6 litres. (d) The gain is 1 litre = ₹1.5 a day; 60 days give ₹90, less than ₹120. Break-even is 120 ÷ 1.5 = 80 days, so do not replant for a 60-day season.
s: Part (c): 6 litres a day for the new row
Part (d): gain 1 litre or ₹1.5 a day, ₹90 in 60 days against ₹120, break-even 80 days, so not worth it

questions.q: Eight stalls at a fair sold tickets worth 212, 450, 389, 601, 640, 733, 120, 410 rupees in this order along one row. A stall is a 'star' if its sales are greater than the stall on each side of it. How many stars are there?

Marks of nine students seated in three rows of three are: row 1: 418, 962, 305; row 2: 777, 530, 849; row 3: 126, 684, 951. A seat is a supercell if its number is greater than the numbers in the seats immediately left, right, in front and behind. How many supercells are there?
Nisha fills a row of 11 cells with 11 different numbers and wants as many supercells as possible. At most how many can she get?
Karan fills a 3 by 3 table with the numbers 1 to 9, each once, in a way of his own. Which cell is certain to be a supercell, however he fills it?
questions.a: The cell holding 9
o: The centre cell, as it has the most neighbours
A corner cell, as it has only two neighbours
The cell holding 8, the second largest

questions.q:
A table is filled with different numbers.
Statement 1: The cell with the largest number is a supercell wherever it is placed.
Statement 2: A corner cell holding the smallest number can be a supercell, because a corner has only two neighbours.
Statement 3: A cell and the cell diagonally below-right of it cannot both be supercells.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The smallest number in a table of different numbers can never be a supercell.
Reason (R): A table of 9 different numbers can have at most 5 supercells.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each table of different numbers in Column I with the largest number of supercells it can have in Column II.
Column I: 1. A row of 7 cells 2. A 2 by 2 table 3. A table of 2 rows and 3 columns 4. A 3 by 3 table
Column II: A. 3 B. 5 C. 4 D. 2
A row of 15 cells filled with different numbers can have at most ___ supercells.
A row holds 52, 170, 98, 98, 60. (a) Which numbers are supercells? (b) The fourth number, 98, is greater than the 60 beside it. Why is it still not a supercell?
questions.a: (a) Only 170, which is greater than 52 and 98. (b) A supercell must be greater than every neighbour, and its other neighbour is also 98, which it does not exceed (equal is not greater).
s: Part (b): 98 is not greater than its other neighbour 98, so it fails the rule

questions.q: A table has 4 rows and 3 columns. (a) How many of its cells have 2 neighbours, how many have 3 and how many have 4? (b) Which kind of cell has the fewest numbers to beat, and does that make it a supercell for certain?
questions.a: (a) Corner cells have 2 neighbours: 4 cells. Edge cells that are not corners have 3: 6 cells. Inner cells have 4: 2 cells (total 12). (b) A corner has the fewest to beat, but it is a supercell only if its number is larger than both neighbours; having fewer neighbours does not decide it.
s: Part (a): 4 cells with 2, 6 cells with 3, 2 cells with 4
Part (b): the corner has the fewest to beat but is not a supercell unless its number is larger

questions.q: True or False: In a table filled with different numbers, the cell holding the largest number is a supercell wherever it is placed.
questions.a: True. All the other numbers are smaller, so the largest number is greater than every neighbour whether it is in a corner, on an edge or inside.
s: Reason: every neighbour holds a smaller number

questions.q: True or False: Two cells that touch only at a corner (diagonal cells) cannot both be supercells.
questions.a: False. Neighbours are only the cells to the left, right, top and bottom, so diagonal cells do not compare with each other. In the table with rows 9, 1 and 2, 8 the cells 9 and 8 are both supercells.
s: Corrects it: diagonal cells are not neighbours, so both can be supercells, with an example

questions.q: In a 3 by 3 table of different numbers, can the second smallest number be a supercell? Give the reason.
questions.a: No. Every cell of a 3 by 3 table has at least 2 neighbours, and only one number, the smallest, is less than the second smallest. So it cannot beat all its neighbours.
s: Says it cannot be a supercell
Reason: it has at least 2 neighbours but only one smaller number exists

questions.q: Anil says that a row of n different numbers can have n ÷ 2 supercells at most, for every n. Test this for n = 7 and n = 8 and say how far he is right.
questions.a: For n = 8 the most is 4 = 8 ÷ 2, so he is right. For n = 7 the most is 4 (cells 1, 3, 5, 7), not 3.5. So he is right only for an even number of cells; for an odd number the most is (n + 1) ÷ 2.
s: Concludes: right for even n only; odd n gives (n + 1) ÷ 2

questions.q: Show that a 2 by 2 table of different numbers cannot have 3 supercells.
questions.a: Choose any 3 of the 4 cells. Two of them share a side, so they are neighbours. Two neighbouring cells cannot both be supercells, since each would have to be greater than the other. So at most 2 supercells are possible.
s: Notes that any 3 of the 4 cells include two side-by-side cells
Each of the two would have to exceed the other
Concludes 3 supercells are impossible (2 at most)

questions.q: Place the seven numbers 210, 345, 470, 505, 620, 688 and 734 in a row of 7 cells so that exactly 4 cells are supercells. Write the row and name the supercells.
questions.a: One row is 734, 210, 688, 345, 620, 470, 505. The supercells are 734, 688, 620 and 505, because each is greater than the cells on its sides (the smaller numbers 210, 345 and 470 sit between them).
s: A row with the four largest numbers in the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th cells
Checks each is greater than its neighbours

questions.q: A 4 by 4 table has rows: 412, 538, 297, 864 / 655, 741, 749, 523 / 380, 907, 461, 615 / 728, 354, 886, 270. (a) List its supercells. (b) How many neighbours does the cell holding 907 have, and is it a supercell? (c) What is the largest number of supercells these 16 numbers can give in some other arrangement? (d) Say how to arrange them to get it.
questions.a: (a) 864, 749, 907, 615, 728, 886. (b) 907 has 4 neighbours (741, 354, 380, 461) and is greater than all of them, so it is a supercell. (c) 8, because no two neighbouring cells can both be supercells and a 4 by 4 table can have at most 8 cells with no two sharing a side. (d) Colour the table like a chessboard; put the eight largest numbers on one colour and the eight smallest on the other. Then every cell of the first colour beats all its neighbours.
s: Part (b): 4 neighbours and 907 is a supercell
Part (c): 8 with the reason that supercells cannot share a side
Part (d): largest eight on one colour of a chessboard pattern, smallest eight on the other

questions.q: Use each of the digits 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8 exactly once in a 5-digit number. (a) Write the largest such number. (b) Write the smallest even such number. (c) Write the smallest such number that is greater than 60,000. (d) Put 87,542, 24,578, 85,472, 72,458 and 78,425 in a row of 5 cells so that exactly 3 cells are supercells, and name them.
questions.a: (a) 87,542. (b) 24,578 (the even digit 8 is kept for the last place and the rest are in ascending order). (c) 72,458 (it must start with 7 because there is no 6, then ascending). (d) 87,542, 24,578, 85,472, 72,458, 78,425: the supercells are 87,542, 85,472 and 78,425, the three greater numbers in the 1st, 3rd and 5th cells.
s: Part (d): a row with the three larger numbers in cells 1, 3, 5, naming the three supercells

questions.q: A class teacher seats nine students in 3 rows of 3 according to their quiz scores. Current scores, row by row: 41, 47, 38 / 44, 36, 49 / 39, 40, 42. A student whose score is greater than all students sitting immediately left, right, in front and behind is a 'table leader' and gets a badge costing ₹30. She has ₹120 for badges. (a) Find the table leaders now. (b) What is the largest number of leaders any seating of these nine scores can give? (c) Write a seating of the same nine scores that gives exactly 4 leaders. (d) Compare the cost of badges for the present seating, the seating with the most leaders and your seating of 4 leaders, and advise the teacher.
questions.a: (a) 47, 44 and 49. (b) 5. (c) [49, 38, 47] / [39, 36, 40] / [44, 41, 42]: the four largest scores in the corners and the smallest in the centre gives exactly 4 leaders. (d) Badges cost ₹90 now (3 leaders), ₹150 for 5 leaders (₹30 over budget) and ₹120 for 4 leaders (exactly the budget). Advise the 4-leader seating, since it gives more leaders than now and stays within ₹120.
s: Part (c): a seating with exactly 4 leaders
Part (d): costs ₹90, ₹150, ₹120 and the advice for the 4-leader seating

questions.q: Marks of 12 students seated in 3 rows of 4 are: 82, 64, 73, 70 / 49, 76, 76, 82 / 64, 52, 52, 91. The teacher asks everyone to colour the supercells, that is, seats whose marks are greater than the seats left, right, in front and behind. Rahul compares each seat only with the seats to its left and right. Sara compares with all four sides but colours a seat even if its marks are equal to a neighbour's. (a) Which seats should be coloured? (b) Which extra seats does Rahul colour? (c) Which extra seat does Sara colour? (d) The teacher can spend extra time with only one of them. Whom should she help first, and what should she tell that student?
questions.a: (a) The seats with 82 (top left), 64 (bottom left) and 91 (bottom right). (b) The 73 in the top row (below it is 76) and the 82 in the middle row (below it is 91, above it is 70). (c) The 76 in the middle row, second seat (its right neighbour is also 76). (d) Rahul made 2 mistakes against Sara's 1, because he ignored the seats in front and behind, so she should help Rahul first and tell him to check all four sides. A counter-view is that Sara's tie error can occur in any table, so she must be told that equal marks are not greater.
s: Part (c): Sara's extra seat, the 76 beside an equal 76
Part (d): chooses a student with the count of mistakes and states the correction for that student

questions.q: On a number line with equal gaps, the marks labelled 36,400 and 36,700 have exactly 3 gaps between them. What is written at the mark that comes next after 36,700?
Rani marks 8 equally spaced points on a number line, starting at 9,995 and going up by 1 each time. How many of the 8 marks are labelled with 5-digit numbers?
A school gives each new student a roll number that must have exactly 3 digits, starting from 100. How many different roll numbers can it give out?
Aman wants the largest 4-digit number whose digits add up to 31. Which number should he write?

About counting numbers and digits:
Statement 1: There are 99 numbers with two digits, because 99 is the biggest of them.
Statement 2: In writing the numbers from 1 to 100, the digit 7 is written 20 times.
Statement 3: The largest 5-digit number whose digit sum is 14 is 95000.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the numbers from 1 to 1000 the digit 7 is written 300 times.
Reason (R): In each of the ones, tens and hundreds places, the digit 7 appears in exactly 100 of the numbers 000 to 999.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each quantity in Column I with its value in Column II.
Column I: 1. Number of 4-digit numbers 2. Digit sum of 6,075 3. Smallest number with digit sum 14 4. Times the digit 7 is written from 1 to 100
Column II: A. 59 B. 20 C. 18 D. 9000
The digit 0 is written ___ times when we write all the numbers from 1 to 100.
A number line has equal gaps, and its marks labelled 25,000 and 26,500 have 3 gaps between them. (a) What is the size of one gap? (b) What are the labels of the two marks between them?
(a) How many 5-digit numbers are there? (b) How many more 5-digit numbers are there than 4-digit numbers, and how does this compare with the number of 4-digit numbers?
questions.a: (a) 90,000 (10,000 to 99,999). (b) 90,000 − 9,000 = 81,000 more; this is 9 times the number of 4-digit numbers.

questions.q: True or False: The digit 7 is written 20 times from 1 to 100, so from 1 to 1000, which is ten times as far, it is written 200 times.
questions.a: False. From 1 to 1000 it is written 300 times, because the 3-digit numbers add a hundreds place in which 7 appears 100 times, besides 100 times each in the ones and tens places. The count does not simply grow ten times.
s: Corrects it to 300 with the reason: three places with 100 sevens each

questions.q: True or False: There are ten times as many 4-digit numbers as 3-digit numbers.
questions.a: True. There are 900 three-digit and 9,000 four-digit numbers, and 9,000 = 10 × 900: the first digit has 9 choices and each of the other digits has 10.

questions.q: (a) Write the smallest 4-digit number whose digits add up to 17. (b) Is it possible for a 3-digit number to be smaller than this and also have digit sum 17? Give one such number if so.
questions.a: (a) 1,079. (b) Yes. Any 3-digit number is smaller than a 4-digit number; for example 179 has digit sum 17.
s: Part (b): yes, with a valid 3-digit example such as 179

questions.q: Salim says that the largest 3-digit number whose digits add up to 14 is 950 and the smallest is 149. Check his claim.
questions.a: He is right. The hundreds digit 9 is the largest, then the tens digit 5 makes 9 + 5 = 14, so 950 is the largest. For the smallest, the hundreds digit is 1, and the other two digits must add to 13, so the tens digit is at least 4 (4 + 9), giving 149.
s: Largest: 9 in the hundreds place, then 5 in the tens place, 0 in the ones place
Smallest: 1 in the hundreds place, then 4 and 9

questions.q: Meher notices that 3-digit numbers with consecutive digits, 123, 234, 345 and so on, have digit sums 6, 9, 12, all multiples of 3. She says the same will happen for all numbers with four consecutive digits. Test her idea with 1234, 2345 and 3456.
questions.a: Digit sums are 10, 14 and 18. Only 18 is a multiple of 3, so the pattern for 3-digit numbers does not continue to 4-digit numbers. She is right about the 3-digit case but wrong to extend it.
s: Only one of three is a multiple of 3
Verdict: right for 3 digits, wrong for 4 digits

questions.q: Show that no 3-digit number has a digit sum of 28.
questions.a: The largest digit is 9, so the greatest digit sum of a 3-digit number is 9 + 9 + 9 = 27. Since 28 is more than 27, no 3-digit number can have it.
s: Finds the greatest digit sum is 27

questions.q: Digits can be used to build numbers with a fixed digit sum. (a) Write the largest 4-digit number with digit sum 20. (b) Write the smallest 4-digit number with digit sum 20. (c) List all the 2-digit numbers with digit sum 11. (d) Show that the numbers in (c) go up in steps of 9 once they are written in order, and explain why this is so.
questions.a: (a) 9,920. (b) 1,199. (c) 29, 38, 47, 56, 65, 74, 83, 92 (8 numbers). (d) Written in order, 29, 38, 47, 56, 65, 74, 83, 92 each rise by 9. Increasing the tens digit by 1 adds 10 and reducing the ones digit by 1 takes away 1, which keeps the digit sum and changes the number by 9.
s: Part (d): steps of 9 explained by +10 and -1

questions.q: Dinesh counts how many times the digit 0 is written while writing the numbers 1 to 1000. (a) How many times does it appear in the ones place? (b) In the tens place it appears only in numbers with 3 or more digits. Count these. (c) In how many numbers does it appear in the hundreds place? (d) Find the total, and explain why the digit 0 gives a different total from the digit 7, which is written 300 times.
questions.a: (a) The ones place is 0 in 10, 20, ..., 1000: 100 numbers. (b) The tens place is 0 in the 3-digit numbers x0y, which are 9 × 10 = 90, and also in 1000: 91. (c) Only 1000: 1. (d) Total = 100 + 91 + 1 = 192. Zero cannot be the first digit of a number, so it is missing from the leading places of 1 to 999, while 7 can appear in every place.
s: Part (d): total 192, with the reason that 0 never leads a number

questions.q: A colony has plots numbered 1 to 500, and a painter charges ₹6 for each digit he paints on the plot boards. (a) How many digits are needed for the plots 1 to 9 and for the plots 10 to 99? (b) How many digits are needed for all 500 plots? (c) Find the total bill. (d) The committee has only ₹8,000. It can either number only the first 480 plots, or ask residents for the extra money. Find the bill for 480 plots and advise the committee.
questions.a: (a) 9 digits for 1 to 9 and 90 × 2 = 180 for 10 to 99. (b) Plots 100 to 500 are 401 plots with 3 digits each = 1,203, so the total is 9 + 180 + 1,203 = 1,392 digits. (c) 1,392 × 6 = ₹8,352, which is ₹352 above the budget. (d) For 480 plots, 381 three-digit plots give 1,143; 9 + 180 + 1,143 = 1,332 digits and ₹7,992, within the budget. Numbering 480 plots fits but leaves 20 plots without boards; asking for ₹352 more numbers all 500. Either is defensible; the committee should say which it values more.
s: Part (d): ₹7,992 for 480 plots, the ₹352 gap, and a justified choice

questions.q: A trekking board shows heights above sea level on a straight line with equal gaps. The marks labelled 3,150 m and 3,450 m have 3 gaps between them. A group starts at the 3,150 m mark and climbs to a hut at 3,720 m. They take 45 minutes to climb each 100 m of height and rest 15 minutes at every mark they reach on the way (not at the start, and not at the hut). Fog is expected 5 hours 45 minutes after they start. (a) What is the gap on the board and what are the two labels between 3,150 m and 3,450 m? (b) Which marks lie between the start and the hut? (c) How long will the climb to the hut take? (d) Will they reach the hut before the fog, and how safe is the margin?
questions.a: (a) The gap is 300 ÷ 3 = 100 m; the labels are 3,250 m and 3,350 m. (b) 3,250, 3,350, 3,450, 3,550 and 3,650 m (five marks); the hut at 3,720 m is not on a mark. (c) Climbing 570 m takes 5.7 × 45 = 256.5 minutes and five rests take 75 minutes, so 331.5 minutes, that is 5 hours 31.5 minutes. (d) The fog comes at 345 minutes, so they reach it with 13.5 minutes to spare; the margin is small, so they should keep rests short or stop at the 3,650 m mark if the group is slow.
s: Part (a): gap 100 m and labels 3,250 and 3,350
Part (d): 13.5 minutes spare and a judgement on the small margin

questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Match each starting number in Column I with the number of steps its Collatz sequence takes to reach 1 (Column II).
Column I: 1. 6 2. 7 3. 8 4. 9
Column II: A. 3 B. 19 C. 8 D. 16
The Collatz sequence from 24 reaches 1 after ___ steps.
(a) Write the Collatz sequence that starts at 26. (b) Use it to say how many numbers in the sequence are odd, apart from the final 1.
questions.a: (a) 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. (b) The odd numbers before 1 are 13 and 5, so 2.

questions.q: (a) Write the Collatz sequences from 10 and from 3. (b) Why does the sequence from 3 end exactly as the sequence from 10 does?
questions.a: (a) From 10: 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. From 3: 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. (b) The sequence from 3 reaches 10 after one step, and the rule depends only on the number you are at, so everything after 10 is the same.
s: Part (b): the sequence from 3 passes through 10 and the next term depends only on the current number

questions.q: True or False: A Collatz sequence from 27 has not reached 1 after 50 steps, so the conjecture is disproved.
questions.a: False. The sequence from 27 takes 111 steps to reach 1. A long sequence does not disprove the conjecture; only a starting number whose sequence never reaches 1 would.
s: Reason: 27 reaches 1 after 111 steps, so it is only a long sequence

questions.q: True or False: If a Collatz sequence reaches any power of 2, it must go on to reach 1.
questions.a: True. A power of 2 is even, and halving it gives the next lower power of 2, and so on down to 2 and then 1.
s: Reason: repeated halving of a power of 2 ends at 1

questions.q: Differentiate between 'the sequence reached 1 for every number we tried' and 'the sequence always reaches 1', and say which one is known for the Collatz rule.
questions.a: The first is a statement about the numbers actually tried; the second is a claim about every whole number. Only the first is known for the Collatz rule; the second is the Collatz Conjecture, which is still unproved.
s: Separates tested cases from a claim for all whole numbers
States that only the first is known and the second is an unproved conjecture

questions.q: Ravi says: 'If I start with an odd number, the rule makes it bigger, so the sequence can never come down to 1.' Test his claim with 5.
questions.a: Starting at 5: 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. The odd step does make 5 into 16, which is bigger, but then the even steps halve it repeatedly and the sequence reaches 1. So his claim is wrong: the odd step increases the number but the later halvings bring it down.
s: Notes the odd step raises the number but the halvings lower it

questions.q: Meena says: 'If I start the Collatz rule at 64, I only ever halve, and I get to 1.' Check whether she is right.
questions.a: She is right. 64 is even, and halving gives 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Every number on the way is a power of 2, so each is even until 1 is reached and the odd rule is never used.
s: Notes all are even, so only halving is used

questions.q: Show that two odd numbers can never come one after the other in a Collatz sequence.
questions.a: Suppose an odd number is followed by another number. The rule triples it and adds 1: tripling an odd number gives an odd number, and adding 1 makes it even. So the next number is even, never odd.
s: Uses the rule for an odd number: multiply by 3, add 1
Tripling an odd number is odd and adding 1 makes it even
Concludes the next number is even, so no two odd numbers are next to each other

questions.q: Write the Collatz sequence starting at 7. (a) Write all its numbers. (b) How many steps does it take to reach 1? (c) What is the largest number it reaches? (d) In how many of the steps was the number tripled and increased by 1, and how many were halvings? (e) At which number does the sequence join the book's sequence that begins at 22?
questions.a: (a) 7, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. (b) 16 steps. (c) 52. (d) The odd numbers 7, 11, 17, 13 and 5 were tripled and increased by 1: 5 steps; the other 11 steps were halvings. (e) It joins at 22, which is its second number.
s: Part (d)-(e): 5 triple-and-add steps, 11 halvings, join at 22

questions.q: Rohan thinks that the bigger the starting number, the more steps the Collatz sequence needs. (a) Find the number of steps for 18. (b) Find the number of steps for 25. (c) Find the number of steps for 32. (d) Does the table support Rohan? (e) Name a sequence feature that explains the result for 32.
questions.a: (a) 18 takes 20 steps. (b) 25 takes 23 steps. (c) 32 takes 5 steps. (d) The steps rise from 18 to 25 but fall for 32, which is bigger than both, so the claim is not supported. (e) 32 is a power of 2, so it is only halved: 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
s: Part (d): the claim is not supported because 32 needs fewer
Part (e): 32 is a power of 2 and is only halved

questions.q: In a maths club game, Anu starts the Collatz rule at 25 and Bala starts at 35. The club wants to pick one scoring rule: 'most steps to reach 1 wins' or 'highest number reached wins'. (a) Find the number of steps for each player. (b) Find the highest number each reaches. (c) Find the sum of all the numbers in each sequence (the total score). (d) Anu likes 'most steps' and Bala likes 'highest number'. Which rule do you recommend, and which player does the total score favour? Use your figures to justify.
questions.a: (a) Anu: 23 steps; Bala: 13 steps. (b) Anu's highest is 88; Bala's is 160. (c) Anu's total is 658; Bala's is 540. (d) 'Most steps' favours Anu (23 against 13); 'highest number' favours Bala (160 against 88); the total favours Anu (658 against 540). Two of the three rules favour Anu, but the choice is a matter of which feature the club values. A recommendation is accepted if it is supported by these figures and the rule is fixed before the starting numbers are chosen.
s: Part (d): states which rule each player prefers, the total favouring Anu, and a justified recommendation

questions.q: A class checks the Collatz rule for every starting number from 1 to 100 and finds that all of them reach 1. The longest one is the sequence from 97, which takes 118 steps, and the highest number any of them reaches is 9,232 (from 27). The sequence from 100 takes 25 steps. (a) How many of the 100 starting numbers failed to reach 1? (b) Write the second and third numbers of the sequence from 100 and say which rule produced each. (c) A student says the conjecture is now proved. Explain what her evidence shows and what it does not. (d) The head teacher offers 3 more hours of computer time to check 101 to 200. Argue whether this is worth doing.
questions.a: (a) None; all 100 reached 1. (b) 100 is even so it is halved to 50, and 50 is halved to 25 (the halving rule both times). (c) It shows that the rule has worked for these 100 numbers, which supports the conjecture; it does not show it for every whole number, so it is not a proof. (d) For: checking more numbers can raise confidence, and one starting number that never reached 1 would disprove the conjecture. Against: no number of checks can prove it, and the 3 hours may be better used. A reasoned answer on either side is accepted.
s: Part (b): 100 to 50 to 25, halving both times
Part (c): supports but does not prove
Part (d): a reasoned argument for or against, noting that a counter-example would disprove

questions.q: The three sections of Class 6 in a school have 38, 41 and 36 students. The school has Classes 6 to 10, five classes in all, and Rani assumes each class has three sections of similar size. Which is the most reasonable estimate of the students in the school?
questions.a: About 600

questions.q: Farah walks 1.2 km to school, and each of her steps is about 60 cm long. Which is the most reasonable estimate of the steps she takes?
questions.a: About 2,000

questions.q: A book has 240 pages, of which about 12 are blank or have pictures only. Which plan gives a reasonable estimate of the number of words in it?
questions.a: Count words on a few typical pages, then multiply by printed pages
o: Count words on a few typical pages, then multiply by printed pages
Count the words on the title page alone, then multiply by all 240 pages
Count the words on the fullest page alone, then multiply by all 240 pages
Count the letters in one line alone, then multiply by all 240 pages

questions.q: Imran has been in school for 6 years, at 6 hours a day and 200 school days a year. Which is the most reasonable estimate of the hours he has spent in school?
questions.a: About 7,200

questions.q:
About estimation:
Statement 1: Two careful people can estimate the same quantity differently and both be reasonable.
Statement 2: An estimate is good only after the exact count has been found.
Statement 3: If one section has 32 students and a school has 15 similar sections, about 500 students is a reasonable estimate.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If one section has 36 students, a school with 12 such sections has about 3,600 students.
Reason (R): To scale up an estimate, we multiply the known amount by the number of similar parts.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: A tap drips 1 drop every 2 seconds. In one hour it drips ___ drops.
Nisha rounds each price to the nearest ten rupees: 5 notebooks at ₹38 each, 4 pens at ₹12 each and a geometry box at ₹98. Her estimated bill, in rupees, is ___.
A tank holds 1,000 litres and a mug holds about 250 millilitres. (a) About how many mugs of water fill the tank? (b) A bucket holds 16 mugs. How many bucketfuls fill the tank?
Mira blinks about 15 times a minute. (a) About how many times does she blink in an hour? (b) About how many times in the 16 hours she is awake?
True or False: If an estimate is different from the exact count, the estimate must be wrong.
questions.a: False. An estimate is not meant to be exact. It is judged by whether the reasoning behind it is sound; for example, 100 is a reasonable estimate for sections of 32, 29 and 35 students even though the exact count is 96.
s: Reason: an estimate is judged by its reasoning, with an example such as 100 for 96

questions.q: Aman estimates the students in his school as 500, using one section of 32 students, 3 sections in each class and 5 classes. Bela estimates 450. Can both be reasonable? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. Aman's working gives 32 × 15 = 480, which rounds to about 500. Bela may have assumed that some sections are smaller. What matters is that each can explain the scaling; neither is exactly right.
s: Bela's lower value is also reasonable if her reasoning is sound

questions.q: A student has studied from Class 1 to Class 6 at 200 school days a year. (a) About how many school days is this? (b) If the school day is 5 hours long, about how many hours is this?
Sonal breathes about 15 times a minute and says she breathes about 2 lakh times in a day. Check her claim.
questions.a: In an hour she breathes 15 × 60 = 900 times, and in a day (24 hours) 900 × 24 = 21,600 times, which is about 20,000. Her figure of 2 lakh is about ten times too large, so the claim is not reasonable.
s: Concludes 2 lakh is about ten times too large

questions.q: Tarun says that a school with 18 sections of about 28 students each has about 500 students. Check his claim.
questions.a: 18 × 28 = 504, which is very close to 500. So his estimate is reasonable, because the section count and size are both used correctly (18 × 30 = 540 would also be reasonable).

questions.q: Make up an estimation question about your own school or town, whose answer is about 6,000. State the quantity you start from and show the scaling.
questions.a: For example: about how many hours does a student spend in school in six years? Start with a 5-hour day, 200 days a year: 5 × 200 = 1,000 hours a year, and 6 × 1,000 = 6,000. (Any consistent question is accepted.)
s: Asks a question that needs an estimate
States the known amount it starts from

questions.q: Karan breathes about 16 times a minute. (a) How many times does he breathe in an hour? (b) How many times in a day? (c) Round your answer in (b) to the nearest thousand to give an estimate. (d) About how many times in a year of 365 days, to the nearest lakh? (e) Karan says he breathes about 8 crore times a year. Is that reasonable?
questions.a: (a) 16 × 60 = 960. (b) 960 × 24 = 23,040. (c) About 23,000. (d) 23,040 × 365 = 84,09,600, which is about 84 lakh. (e) 8 crore is 800 lakh, about ten times the estimate of 84 lakh, so it is not reasonable.
s: Part (e): compares 1 crore with 84 lakh and gives a judgement

questions.q: Rani lives 2.4 km from school and each step of hers is about 60 cm. (a) About how many steps does she take to school? (b) She walks about 100 steps a minute. About how long does the walk take? (c) She goes to school and back 6 days a week. About how many steps is that in a week? (d) She wants to walk 10,000 steps a day. How many more steps a day does she need on school days?
questions.a: (a) 2.4 km = 2,400 m = 240,000 cm, and 240,000 ÷ 60 = 4,000 steps. (b) 4,000 ÷ 100 = 40 minutes. (c) 4,000 × 2 × 6 = 48,000 steps. (d) She walks 8,000 steps a day, so she needs 10,000 − 8,000 = 2,000 more steps a day.

questions.q: A class of 40 children is to share a fruit custard. For every 8 children the recipe needs 1 litre of milk at ₹58, 1 kg of bananas at ₹48, 1 kg of apples at ₹180 and half a kg of grapes at ₹120 a kg. The class has ₹1,600. (a) How many groups of 8 are there? (b) Find the exact cost for all 40 children. (c) Estimate the cost by rounding each item's cost for one group to the nearest ten rupees, and give the difference from the exact cost. (d) Compare the options: leave out the grapes, or keep everything and collect the extra money. Recommend one.
questions.a: (a) 40 ÷ 8 = 5 groups. (b) One group costs 58 + 48 + 180 + 60 = ₹346, so 5 groups cost ₹1,730. (c) Rounded: 60 + 50 + 180 + 60 = ₹350 per group, ₹1,750 in all, ₹20 more than the exact cost. (d) Without grapes: 5 × 286 = ₹1,430, inside ₹1,600 with ₹170 left. With everything: ₹1,730, so ₹130 more must be collected. Leaving out the grapes needs no collection but loses a fruit; collecting ₹130 (₹3.25 a child) keeps the recipe. Either is acceptable with reasons.
s: Part (c): estimate ₹1,750, ₹20 above the exact cost
Part (d): ₹1,430 without grapes, ₹130 extra with them, and a reasoned recommendation

questions.q: For the annual day, the school sets out chairs in 8 equal blocks, and one block has 10 rows with 12 chairs in each. Another 150 people are expected to stand. Food packets cost ₹18 each if ordered now, and ₹25 each if bought at the last minute. (a) How many chairs are there? (b) If every chair is taken, about how many people attend? (c) If one chair in five stays empty, about how many attend? (d) The school can order 1,000 or 1,200 packets now. Find the cost of each order, and the extra cost of last-minute packets if all chairs are taken and the order was 1,000. Recommend an order.
questions.a: (a) 8 × 10 × 12 = 960 chairs. (b) 960 + 150 = 1,110 people. (c) 4 of every 5 chairs are used: 768 + 150 = 918 people. (d) 1,000 packets cost ₹18,000 and 1,200 cost ₹21,600. If 1,110 attend, 110 packets are short; at ₹25 these cost ₹2,750, so 1,000 plus last-minute packets costs ₹20,750, still less than ₹21,600. Ordering 1,000 is cheaper in both cases, but 1,200 removes the risk of running short; either is acceptable if the school states how much risk it accepts.
s: Part (d): ₹18,000, ₹21,600, extra ₹2,750 and a justified order

questions.q: Two players take turns adding 1, 2, 3 or 4 to a running total, starting from 0, and whoever reaches exactly 30 wins. Who can force a win with correct play?
questions.a: The second player, by completing each round to 5
o: The second player, by completing each round to 5
The first player, by saying 1 and then adding 4 every turn
The first player, because 30 is an even number
Neither player, since the result depends only on luck

questions.q: In a game to reach 29, each turn adds 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 to the total, starting from 0. What should the first player say to be sure of winning?
In the game to 21 (adding 1, 2 or 3 each turn), your opponent has just said 13. What is true of your position?
questions.a: You cannot force a win if the opponent plays correctly
o: You cannot force a win if the opponent plays correctly
You can force a win by saying 14 and then playing carefully
You can force a win by saying 15 and then playing carefully
You can force a win by saying 16 and then playing carefully

questions.q: Players add 1, 2 or 3 to a total starting from 0 and the first to reach the target wins. The target 21 gives the first player a winning strategy. Which new target would let the second player win with correct play?

About counting games in which each turn adds a number from 1 up to a fixed limit and the first to reach the target wins:
Statement 1: In the game to 21 with adds of 1 to 3, the second player can always win.
Statement 2: In the game to 99 with adds of 1 to 10, the second player can always win.
Statement 3: If the target is a multiple of (the largest add + 1), the second player can always win.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the game to 99 with adds of 1 to 10, the first player can win by saying 11 first.
Reason (R): The safe numbers in this game are 11, 22, 33, and so on up to 99.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q:
In each game in Column I, the players add a number from 1 up to the stated limit and the first to reach the target wins. Match the game with the safe number just below the target (Column II).
Column I: 1. Target 21, adds 1 to 3 2. Target 50, adds 1 to 4 3. Target 99, adds 1 to 10 4. Target 30, adds 1 to 5
Column II: A. 45 B. 24 C. 17 D. 88
In the game to reach 22 by adding 1, 2 or 3 each turn from 0, the first player should say ___ first.
In a game to reach 33, each turn adds 1, 2, 3 or 4 to the total, starting from 0. (a) List the safe numbers. (b) Which player wins with correct play, and what is the first move?
questions.a: (a) 33, 28, 23, 18, 13, 8 and 3 (5 apart). (b) The first player wins by saying 3, and then returning to the next safe number each turn.
s: Part (b): the first player wins, saying 3 first

questions.q: In a game to reach 36, each turn adds 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, starting from 0. (a) Who can force a win? (b) If the first player says 4, what should the second player say, and why?
questions.a: (a) The second player, because 36 is a multiple of 6. (b) The second player says 2, making the total 6, a safe number, since the two numbers always add up to 6.
s: Part (a): the second player, as 36 is a multiple of 6
Part (b): says 2 to make the total 6

questions.q: True or False: In every game of this kind with adds of 1, 2 or 3, the first player can force a win.
questions.a: False. When the target is a multiple of 4, such as 24, the second player wins: whatever the first player says, the second player can bring the total to the next multiple of 4.
s: Gives a counter-example such as target 24 and explains the second player's reply

questions.q: True or False: In the game to 21 with adds of 1, 2 or 3, the player who says 17 can force a win.
questions.a: True. 17 is a safe number: whatever the opponent adds (1, 2 or 3) to reach 18, 19 or 20, the player can add 3, 2 or 1 to reach 21.
s: Reason: from 18, 19 or 20 the player can reach 21 at once

questions.q: Choose a target for a game with adds of 1 to 5 so that the first player wins by saying 2 first. List the safe numbers.
questions.a: Take the target 26 (26 = 4 × 6 + 2). The safe numbers are 26, 20, 14, 8 and 2, each 6 apart, so the first player says 2.

questions.q: Ria says: 'In the game to 99 with adds of 1 to 10, the first player wins by saying 11 first, and then 22, 33 and so on.' Check her claim.
questions.a: She is wrong. The first player may only say a number from 1 to 10, so 11 is not allowed as the first move. Whatever the first player says, the second player can add the rest to make 11. So the second player wins.
s: States the first number must be from 1 to 10, so 11 is not allowed
Shows the second player can bring the total to 11

questions.q: Sam says: 'In the game to 26 with adds of 1 to 4, the first player wins by saying 1.' Check his claim.
questions.a: He is right. The safe numbers are 26, 21, 16, 11, 6 and 1, each 5 apart. By saying 1 the first player is on a safe number and can return to the next safe number after every reply.
s: Notes that saying 1 puts the first player on a safe number

questions.q: Show that in the game to 20 with adds of 1, 2 or 3, the first player cannot force a win against a player who plays correctly.
questions.a: 20 is a multiple of 4. Whatever the first player adds (1, 2 or 3), the second player adds 3, 2 or 1, so each round totals 4: 4, 8, 12, 16 and then 20. The second player reaches 20 first.
s: Shows the second player can always make each round add up to 4
Concludes the second player reaches 20, so the first cannot force a win

questions.q: A game is played to reach 50, each turn adding any number from 1 to 6 to the total, starting from 0. (a) Write the safe numbers. (b) Who can force a win and with what first move? (c) The first player says 1 and the second says 5, making 6. What should the first player say next? (d) If the target is changed to 49, who can force a win now, and why?
questions.a: (a) 50, 43, 36, 29, 22, 15, 8 and 1 (7 apart). (b) The first player, by saying 1. (c) 8, by adding 2 to 6. (d) 49 is a multiple of 7, so the second player wins: whatever the first player says, the second player makes each round add up to 7.
s: Part (b): the first player wins, saying 1
Part (d): second player wins as 49 is a multiple of 7, with the reply rule

questions.q: In a game where each turn adds 1, 2, 3 or 4 and the first to reach the target wins, the target may be any number from 20 to 30. (a) For which targets does the second player win? (b) For target 28, write the safe numbers and the first move. (c) For target 24, what is the first move? (d) State the rule that tells you who wins, without playing.
questions.a: (a) 20, 25 and 30. (b) 28, 23, 18, 13, 8 and 3; the first move is 3. (c) The safe numbers for 24 are 24, 19, 14, 9 and 4, so the first player says 4. (d) Look at the remainder when the target is divided by 5: if it is 0, the second player wins; otherwise the first player wins by saying that remainder first.
s: Part (b): safe numbers and first move 3
Part (d): remainder 0 means the second player wins, otherwise the first move is the remainder

questions.q: A teacher wants two counting games for a 10-minute activity, one where the first player wins and one where the second player wins. Each move takes about 15 seconds, and she can give each game 4 minutes (240 seconds). Game A: target 21, adds 1 to 3. Game B: target 99, adds 1 to 10. Game C: target 30, adds 1 to 4. When the winner always returns to a safe number, each round adds exactly one more than the largest allowed add, so the number of moves does not depend on how the loser plays. (a) Who wins each game with correct play? (b) Find the number of moves in each game. (c) Find the time each game takes. (d) Which two games should she choose?
questions.a: (a) A: the first player (21 is not a multiple of 4); B: the second player (99 is a multiple of 11); C: the second player (30 is a multiple of 5). (b) A: the first player says 1, and 20 more is 5 rounds of 2 moves, so 11 moves; B: 9 rounds of 2 moves, 18 moves; C: 6 rounds of 2 moves, 12 moves. (c) A: 11 × 15 = 165 s; B: 18 × 15 = 270 s; C: 12 × 15 = 180 s. (d) B is over 240 s, so she should choose A (first player wins) and C (second player wins), both within 240 s.
s: Part (a): first wins A, second wins B and C
Part (d): chooses A and C because B exceeds 240 s and the pair gives one of each kind of winner

questions.q: In the game to 21 (each turn adds 1, 2 or 3, first to reach 21 wins), Pia and Qadir played, and the totals after each move were 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 17, 20, 21. Pia moved first and Qadir second. (a) Which of the totals said by each player were safe numbers? (b) Which move first took control away from the player who had it? (c) What should Qadir have said when the total stood at 7? (d) Pia says 'I won because my first move, 2, was the best.' Judge her statement using the totals.
questions.a: (a) The safe numbers are 1, 5, 9, 13, 17 and 21. Qadir said 5 (safe); Pia said 9, 13, 17 and 21. (b) Qadir's move from 7 to 8 gave up control, since he should have reached 9. (c) He should have said 9 (adding 2). (d) Her first move of 2 was not a safe number, since the safe first move is 1, and Qadir took control at 5. She won because Qadir missed 9, not because 2 was the best first move.
s: Part (d): her first move was not safe, and Qadir's mistake decided the game
